Bone Lesions in a Child

bone lesions by site, age and periosteum · the aggressive film and MRI before biopsy · Ewing sarcoma or osteomyelitis · natural history · treatment by cause

1Presentation
Bottom line
  • Sunburst periosteum or a Codman triangle at the metaphysis near the knee in a teenager: osteosarcoma. Onion skin in the shaft or pelvis, sometimes with fever: Ewing sarcoma
  • An aggressive film gets MRI of the bone, then the biopsy; chest CT stages the lungs. Fever does not exclude a tumor
  • Benign lesions are named by site and age and observed: a painless spur is an osteochondroma; night pain relieved by a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) is an osteoid osteoma; a central metaphyseal lucency is a unicameral bone cyst (simple bone cyst)
What it is

A bone lesion on a child's plain film, named by where it sits, the child's age and the periosteum

Sort by

The site (epiphysis, metaphysis or shaft), then the age (physes open or closed), then the periosteum (quiet, or aggressive: sunburst, Codman triangle, onion skin) Ewing sarcoma or osteosarcomaFever, leukocytosis and high inflammatory markers occur in Ewing sarcoma and often mean it has spread; osteosarcoma rarely brings them

Hands off

Leukemia, the febrile limp, one-sided leg pain and the mass after an injury have their own briefs

2Urgent risks
OsteosarcomaA painful, enlarging mass near the knee in a teenager, or a pathologic fracture

If the film shows sunburst periosteum or a Codman triangle, choose MRI of the bone, then biopsy; chest CT for lung metastases.

Ewing sarcomaWeeks of pain and swelling in the shaft or pelvis; fever and high markers can mimic infection

If the film shows a permeative lytic lesion with onion-skin layers, choose MRI, then biopsy; fever does not exclude it.

OsteomyelitisDays of fever with point tenderness at a long-bone metaphysis; the film is normal early

If the child is febrile and the bone is tender, choose CBC, ESR (erythrocyte sedimentation rate), CRP (C-reactive protein) and blood culture.

LeukemiaBone pain with fever, pallor or bruising, and no lytic lesion on the film

If the film shows no lesion and the child is pale or bruised, choose CBC with peripheral smear.

3Differential
Aggressive film or a painful bone, most tempting first
DiagnosisFingerprintDecides it
Ewing sarcomaPeak 10 to 15, more often boys; pain and swelling in the shaft, pelvis or axial skeleton; fever, leukocytosis and high markers in someWeeks: permeative, moth-eaten lytic lesion with onion-skin (lamellated) periosteum; biopsy: sheets of small round blue cells; t(11;22)
OsteosarcomaTeens; painful enlarging mass at the distal femur or proximal tibia; rarely febrile; prior radiation or hereditary retinoblastomaChronic, progressive pain: metaphyseal lesion, lytic and sclerotic, with sunburst periosteum and a Codman triangle; high alkaline phosphatase (ALP) and lactate dehydrogenase; biopsy: osteoid-producing cells
Osteomyelitis
Fever, focal pain and swelling; long-bone metaphysis; trauma or immunodeficiency support itDays: point tenderness; the film turns abnormal after 2 to 4 weeks; biopsy: inflammatory cells and necrotic bone
Acute lymphoblastic leukemia
Bone pain with fever, pallor or bruisingNo lytic lesion: the pain comes from the marrow; cytopenias on the CBC with smear
Langerhans cell histiocytosisChildren; bone and skinLytic lesion with a pathologic fracture and no skin disease (eosinophilic granuloma); lytic skull lesions with a scalp rash, diabetes insipidus (arginine vasopressin deficiency) and exophthalmos; biopsy: S-100 stain
ChondrosarcomaAdults, over 40 to 50; pelvis, proximal femur or humerusGrowth of an osteochondroma after the physes close suggests it; ring-and-arc calcifications
Quiet lesion on a film, most tempting first
DiagnosisFingerprintDecides it
Osteoid osteomaTeens, more often boys; proximal femur most often, or the spineNight pain unrelated to activity, relieved by NSAIDs; nidus under 2 cm in a sclerotic rim; CT shows the nidus best
Unicameral bone cyst (simple bone cyst)Physes open; humerus or femur; painless and incidental, or a pathologic fractureCentral metaphyseal lucency, narrow transition zone, no periosteal reaction
OsteochondromaTeens; the most common benign bone tumor; a painless hard bump near the knee; multiple if hereditarySpur from the metaphysis pointing away from the joint, continuous with the cortex and medulla
Nonossifying fibromaCommon in children; femur or tibia; found by chance on a filmWell-circumscribed lytic lesion, no symptoms
ChondroblastomaAge 10 to 21, more often boys, physes open; distal femur, proximal tibia or proximal humerus; constant joint painEpiphyseal lucency with a thin sclerotic rim; may cross the physis
Giant cell tumor of bone (osteoclastoma)Age 20 to 40, skeletally mature; distal femur or proximal tibia; joint pain and swellingEccentric, expansile lytic lesion in the epiphysis with a soap-bubble look
Aneurysmal bone cystAdolescents; rapid growthExpansile lytic lesion with a thin sclerotic rim; MRI shows fluid-fluid levels
Site and age
SiteLesion
EpiphysisChondroblastoma (physes open); giant cell tumor (mature)
MetaphysisOsteochondroma, unicameral bone cyst, osteosarcoma, nonossifying fibroma
Shaft (diaphysis)Ewing sarcoma; osteoid osteoma
PelvisEwing sarcoma in a child; chondrosarcoma in an adult
4Workup
Treatment by cause
CauseTreatment
OsteochondromaObserve; excision if it grows, hurts or disturbs growth Osteochondromaboard sources teach about 1%; a standard clinical reference puts malignant change at well under 1% of single osteochondromas
Osteoid osteomaNSAIDs and serial films until it resolves Osteoid osteomaradiofrequency ablation of the nidus gives lasting relief in most cases
Unicameral bone cyst (simple bone cyst)Observe with serial films until it resolves; the risk is fracture Unicameral bone cystsmaller cysts sometimes heal on their own; larger cysts in children may need an intervention
Nonossifying fibromaObserve
ChondroblastomaCurettage and bone grafting
Giant cell tumor of bone (osteoclastoma)Curettage or excision; high local recurrence; denosumab if unresectable
Aneurysmal bone cystResection
OsteosarcomaChemotherapy plus en bloc resection
Ewing sarcomaChemotherapy plus resection, with or without radiation
Clues that change the answer
CluePoints toNext move
Fever with a lytic lesion over weeksEwing sarcoma, not only osteomyelitisMRI, then biopsy
Night pain that an NSAID relievesOsteoid osteoma: the nidus makes prostaglandinsRadiograph; CT for the nidus
Fracture through a lucent lesion after a minor fallUnicameral bone cyst; eosinophilic granuloma if lytic with no skin diseaseSerial radiographs for a classic cyst
An osteochondroma that grows after the physes closeChondrosarcomaExcision or biopsy
Bone pain with cytopenias and a normal filmLeukemia
CBC with smear
Pause point
Febrile lytic lesion Offered as osteomyelitis Name the site, the age and the periosteum → Not osteomyelitis on fever alone
A lesion the film already names Offered: biopsy A benign name → Observed
Sunburst or onion skin on the film Offered: repeating the film An aggressive film → MRI, then biopsy
Practice
  1. 12-year-old girl: pelvic film shows a moth-eaten lytic lesion of the right ilium with lamellated periosteal reaction Tender mass over the right buttock, growing for 6 weeks T 38.4 °C · leukocytes 12,800/mm³ · biopsy: sheets of small round blue cells → Ewing sarcoma → a pelvic lytic lesion over weeks with layered periosteum is Ewing sarcoma: MRI maps it, and biopsy shows uniform small round blue cells in sheets, little cytoplasm, fibrous septa; osteomyelitis can also bring fever but favors long bones, and its biopsy shows inflammatory cells and necrotic bone, and osteosarcoma is metaphyseal, rarely pelvic and rarely febrile
  2. 13-year-old girl, painless hard bump above the left knee 3 weeks; unchanged no trauma, fever or weight loss Firm, nontender distal femoral mass Vital signs normal · film: metaphyseal spur pointing away from the joint, continuous with cortex and medulla → Grows until the growth plates close, then stops → a spur continuous with the cortex and medulla is an osteochondroma, the most common benign bone tumor: it grows with the skeleton until physeal closure, then stops; transformation is about 1% and involution belongs to osteoid osteoma
  3. 15-year-old boy with 2 months of right thigh pain worst at night; unrelated to activity ibuprofen relieves it completely No weight loss or limp Afebrile · film: small round lucency with a sclerotic rim, proximal femur → Osteoid osteoma → night pain relieved by NSAIDs with a small lucent nidus in a sclerotic rim is osteoid osteoma, most often in the proximal femur
  4. 16-year-old boy was diagnosed with osteoid osteoma of the femur 2 months ago night pain controlled by ibuprofen no other complaints Parents ask what happens if nothing more is done Afebrile · repeat film unchanged → Spontaneous involution → osteoid osteoma resolves on its own, so NSAIDs and serial films are reasonable
  5. 14-year-old boy was diagnosed with osteoid osteoma of the tibia last week pain wakes him at night one ibuprofen dose stops it within an hour Parents ask why the medicine works so well Afebrile · nidus under 2 cm on film → Prostaglandin production by the nidus → the nidus makes prostaglandins, which NSAIDs block, so the response is nearly diagnostic
  6. 13-year-old girl with 6 weeks of worsening pain below the knee firm mass over the proximal tibia no trauma Pain now present at rest Afebrile · film: mixed lytic and dense metaphyseal lesion, sunburst periosteal reaction → Osteosarcoma → a metaphyseal mixed lesion with a sunburst reaction in a teenager is osteosarcoma, the most common primary bone malignancy of childhood; prior radiation and hereditary retinoblastoma raise the risk
  7. 15-year-old boy with 6 weeks of progressive pain above the right knee now wakes him at night firm, tender distal thigh swelling Film: ill-defined mixed lytic-sclerotic distal femoral metaphysis Afebrile · sunburst reaction, Codman triangle · ALP elevated → MRI of the right femur → an aggressive film gets MRI of the whole involved extremity before biopsy: it maps soft tissue and vessels and plans the biopsy; chest CT stages the lungs
  8. 12-year-old boy with 6 weeks of worsening thigh pain wakes him at night intermittent fevers; lost 2 kg; no trauma or recent infection Film: moth-eaten mid-shaft femoral lysis, onion-skin periosteum T 38.2 °C · ESR 55 mm/h → Ewing sarcoma → a permeative diaphyseal lesion with onion-skin layers over weeks, with weight loss, is Ewing sarcoma; the shaft and the 6-week course argue against osteomyelitis; fever, when present, often means it has spread
  9. 7-year-old boy, febrile 4 days won't bear weight on left leg warm, point-tender distal femoral metaphysis; full, painless knee motion MRI: marrow edema, small subperiosteal collection T 39.2 °C · WBC 16,000/mm³, neutrophils · hemoglobin, platelets normal · CRP markedly high · film normal → Osteomyelitis → days of fever with metaphyseal point tenderness and an early normal film is osteomyelitis: blood culture, intravenous antibiotics, drain the abscess; Ewing sarcoma runs for weeks
  10. 9-year-old boy with arm pain after a minor fall no pain before the fall tender upper arm Fracture through a well-defined central proximal humeral metaphyseal lucency Afebrile · thin sclerotic margin; no periosteal reaction → Unicameral bone cyst → a central metaphyseal lucency with no periosteal reaction that fractures is a unicameral bone cyst; medullary expansion thins the cortex; chondroblastoma is also a lucency with a sclerotic rim, but it sits in the epiphysis
  11. 10-year-old girl, mild shoulder pain after a fall on an outstretched hand full range of motion no weight loss No fracture on film Afebrile · incidental well-defined central proximal humeral metaphyseal lucency · thin cortex; narrow transition; no periosteal reaction → Observation with serial radiographs → an incidental unicameral bone cyst is observed with serial films; it resolves by physeal closure, and the risk is pathologic fracture
  12. 28-year-old woman with 4 months of knee pain and swelling skeletally mature no trauma, fever or weight loss Eccentric expansile lytic lesion of the distal femoral epiphysis Afebrile · soap-bubble appearance on film → Giant cell tumor of bone → an expansile soap-bubble epiphyseal lesion after skeletal maturity is giant cell tumor: locally destructive, curettage or excision, high local recurrence
  13. 16-year-old boy with 3 months of constant knee pain physes still open; no weight loss mild joint swelling Well-circumscribed epiphyseal lucency, thin sclerotic rim, crossing the physis Afebrile · no periosteal reaction → Chondroblastoma → an epiphyseal lucency before skeletal maturity is chondroblastoma; age separates it from giant cell tumor; curettage
Pairs with Leg Pain in a Child: one-sided night pain needs a film. Muscle Contusion and Myositis Ossificans: the post-injury mass. Acute Leukemia in a Child: bone pain from marrow. The Limping Child: the febrile limp.
Transferable rule

To predict a lesion's course, name it first, then recall what it does. To name it, check site, age and fever before reading the film.
